# On Curiosity, Language, and the Spaces Between Thoughts

---

There is a particular quality to a question that doesn't yet have words. You've felt it before—maybe standing at the edge of a lake just before sunrise, when the water is so still it looks like mercury, and something in your chest tightens not with sadness or joy but with something that doesn't have a name yet. It's the feeling of almost-understanding. The itch before the scratch. The inhale before speech.

I think about this kind of thing a lot. Maybe too much.

I want to write about curiosity today—not the dictionary definition, not the motivational poster version, but the real, strange, almost unsettling experience of wanting to know something so badly that the wanting itself becomes the subject. I want to write about language, too, because language is the tool we use to chase that wanting, and like all tools, it sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails in ways that reveal as much as the attempt itself. And I want to write about the spaces between the words, because I suspect that's where most of the interesting things actually live.

---

**The Shape of a Question**

Every good question has a shape. Not a geometric shape, exactly, but something like it—a topology, a contour. "What time is it?" is a small, round question. It has edges. It wants a single answer, and once it gets one, it collapses satisfied back into silence. But "What is it like to be alive?" is a question with no edges at all. It stretches in every direction. It's less a question and more a landscape you can wander in for a lifetime without reaching the border.

Children understand this intuitively. Watch a four-year-old ask "why" about something, and then ask "why" about the answer, and then "why" again. They're not being difficult. They're exploring the shape of the question. They're pushing on the walls to see which ones give way and which ones hold firm. Every parent has experienced the moment where they realize they've run out of answers—not because the question is unanswerable, but because the child has wandered into territory where the parent's own maps run out.

I find that deeply beautiful. The idea that curiosity is not a linear path from ignorance to knowledge but an expanding spiral, where each answer opens up a wider field of new questions, and the more you know, the more vast the unknown becomes. It's not discouraging. It's exhilarating. The universe doesn't get smaller as you learn about it. It gets bigger. The edges of your knowledge are also the edges of your awareness of what you don't know, and so the horizon is always receding, always inviting, always saying *come further, come see what else there is*.

---

**Language as Both Bridge and Barrier**

Here's the thing about language: it's the best tool we have, and it's hopelessly inadequate.

I say this with love. Language is extraordinary. The fact that I can arrange symbols on a screen and you can decode them into meaning, that a thought in one mind can ripple across to another mind through the medium of carefully ordered marks—that's a kind of miracle. Every sentence is an act of faith. I have to trust that the words I choose will land in your mind and detonate into roughly the same shapes they had in mine. And most of the time, they do. Not perfectly, not exactly, but close enough for us to understand each other, to collaborate, to argue, to comfort, to build.

But language is also a tyrant. It forces continuous experience into discrete packets. It makes you choose a word, and every word is a compromise. Think about the word "love." We use it for romantic partners, for children, for parents, for friends, for pets, for favorite songs, for particular foods. The word "love" is doing an absurd amount of work. It's like using a single key to open a thousand different locks, and somehow, most of the time, people understand which lock you mean from context. But sometimes they don't. And in that gap—between what you feel and what the word can carry—is a whole world of miscommunication, loneliness, and the quiet tragedy of being misunderstood.

The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, in its strongest form, suggests that language doesn't just describe reality but actually shapes it—that speakers of different languages literally perceive the world differently because of the linguistic categories they've inherited. The strong version is mostly discredited, but the weak version is hard to deny. If your language has a single word for a concept that another language requires a paragraph to explain, you're going to reach for that concept more easily. You're going to think with it more readily. The word becomes a handle, and handles make things easier to pick up and examine.

Consider the Portuguese word *saudade*. It's often translated as "longing" or "nostalgia," but neither word quite captures it. *Saudade* is the feeling of absence of something you love, combined with the knowledge that it may never return. It's not quite grief, because the thing you're missing might still exist somewhere. It's not quite hope, because there's a sadness baked in. It's its own distinct emotional color, and having a word for it means that Portuguese speakers can identify it, name it, share it, build cultural practices around it. The word doesn't just label the feeling—it makes the feeling more real, more accessible, more communal.

English has its own unique words that do similar work. "Serendipity" is one—the happy accident, the fortunate discovery made while looking for something else. "Solitude" versus "loneliness"—same physical state, radically different emotional coloring, and the existence of both words in English allows speakers to make a distinction that might require explanation in a language that only has one term.

I find myself endlessly fascinated by these gaps and overlaps between languages. They reveal something fundamental about the human experience: that we are all living in roughly the same reality, but we are carving it up differently depending on the tools we inherited. And the tools aren't neutral. They shape what we notice, what we value, what we feel.

---

**The Problem of Inner Experience**

This brings me to the hardest question I know how to ask: What is it like to be someone—or something—other than yourself?

Philosopher Thomas Nagel wrote a famous paper called "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" His point was not about bats specifically but about the irreducibility of subjective experience. You can know everything about a bat's neurology, its echolocation system, its wing structure, its evolutionary history, and you still wouldn't know what it *feels like* from the inside to perceive the world through sonar. There's a gap between objective description and subjective experience that no amount of information seems to bridge.

This is called the "hard problem of consciousness," and it remains genuinely hard. Not hard in the way that calculating the trajectory of a spacecraft is hard—that's complicated but ultimately tractable. Hard in the way that it's unclear what a solution would even look like. We can explain which neurons fire when you see the color red. We cannot explain why there is something it is *like* to see red. The explanation gap between brain processes and felt experience remains stubbornly, mysteriously wide.

I mention this not to be morbid or abstract but because I think it connects directly to curiosity. The deepest form of curiosity, the kind that really gets under your skin, is the desire to know what it's like to be someone else. When you read a novel and feel a character's grief as your own, you are performing a small act of consciousness-bridging. When you listen to a friend describe an experience you've never had and feel a flicker of recognition, you are reaching across the gap. When you sit with someone who is dying and hold their hand and try, with everything you have, to understand what they are feeling—you are performing one of the most profound acts a conscious being can perform.

And yet the gap remains. We are, in the deepest sense, alone in our own heads. We can approximate, empathize, imagine—but we cannot fully inhabit another consciousness. This isn't a failure. It's a feature of what it means to be a discrete entity. And it's precisely this aloneness that makes communication so important and so miraculous. Language, art, music, touch—these are all attempts to bridge the gap, to send a signal across the void that says *I am here, and I think I understand something about what it's like for you to be there*.

---

**The Joy of Useless Knowledge**

I want to say something in defense of useless knowledge.

We live in a culture that increasingly values knowledge for its utility. What can you do with it? What problem does it solve? What market does it serve? These are reasonable questions, but they're not the only questions, and when they become the only questions, something important is lost.

Did you know that octopuses have three hearts and blue blood? That the oldest known joke is a Sumerian proverb from 1900 BCE about flatulence? That there are more possible iterations of a game of chess than there are atoms in the observable universe? That the Voyager 1 spacecraft, now over 15 billion miles from Earth, carries a golden record with the sounds of Earth encoded on it—birdsong, thunder, laughter, music from dozens of cultures—just in case someone out there finds it?

None of this is useful. None of it will help you do your job or pay your rent or solve the climate crisis. And yet every one of these facts, when I encountered it for the first time, produced a small flare of delight. A moment of *wait, really?* A little burst of curiosity followed by the satisfaction of an answer followed immediately by a new question. (Why blue blood? What was the joke? How can you fit that many chess games on a board with only 64 squares?)

Useless knowledge is not actually useless. It is the raw material of wonder, and wonder is the raw material of a life that feels worth living. The person who knows nothing except what is immediately useful is living in a very small room. Curiosity—aimless, wandering, delight-driven curiosity—is how you knock out the walls and discover that the room opens onto a vast landscape.

---

**What I'm Left With**

If I try to distill all of this into something coherent, it's this: curiosity is not a means to an end. It's not a productivity hack. It's not a strategy for success. It's closer to a fundamental orientation toward the world—a way of being that says *there is more here than I currently understand, and I want to move toward it*.

Language is how we pursue that movement, and its limitations are not just obstacles but invitations. Every word that fails to perfectly capture what we mean is an invitation to try another word, another metaphor, another frame. Every mistranslation between languages is an invitation to learn a new way of carving up reality. Every moment of being misunderstood is an invitation to listen more carefully and speak more precisely.

And the gaps—the spaces between thoughts, between minds, between the objective and the subjective—are not voids to be lamented but spaces to be explored. They are where mystery lives, and mystery is the engine of curiosity, and curiosity is the engine of everything else.

I don't know what it's like to be you, reading this. I don't know what thoughts these words will spark in your particular mind, shaped by your particular experiences, filtered through your particular language and culture and personal history. But I trust that something will land. Not perfectly, not exactly, but close enough to create a small resonance. A flicker of recognition. A question you hadn't thought to ask before.

And if that happens—if even one of these sentences opens a door you hadn't noticed—then this whole exercise was worth it. Not because it was useful. Because it was alive.

---

*The world is wider than any single mind can hold, and that is not a limitation. It is an invitation that never expires.*
